intro: To find a hospital policy quickly, skip the home page. Go straight to the policy library, then search with one short phrase or the policy number. Many nurses lose time by searching too broadly or clicking through folders from memory. This guide covers what that costs, why it happens, and fixes you can use today without buying anything.
tldr: Go straight to the policy library, and search with a policy number or a short phrase from the title.
Bookmark the library and the policies you use most in Chrome with ⌘D, so you stop hunting for the search page.
Use ⌘F to find a section inside a long policy, instead of scrolling past it.
Check the revision and effective dates before you act. Old copies can look official.
Lazur can point at the search box and guide you one click at a time. It does not click for you.

blocks.text: What a slow policy search costs you

Nobody logs the minutes spent hunting for a policy, so the cost hides inside the shift. The closest data comes from broader surveys of nurses. In one single-hospital survey, 42.6% of nurses said they were too busy to find time to search for information. That survey had 136 returned responses, and its authors say the results cannot be generalized. Still, the pattern will feel familiar on most units.

The Finnish numbers are the most direct we have. A 2024 study of home care organizations found registered nurses spent about 518 minutes a week on health information management. Of that, 137 minutes went to retrieval, or 25.7% of the time. It was home care, not hospital work, so treat it as a rough signal. It is not a measure of your ward.

Put a price on it if that helps. The Bureau of Labor Statistics lists the median RN pay at $46.90 an hour, based on May 2025 data. At that rate, 137 minutes is about $107 of paid time a week. That is a thought experiment, not an audit. Your own week will look different, and your employer keeps its own numbers.

blocks.text: The honest read is this. The time loss is real, but the research is thin. Use these figures to argue for a fix on your unit, not to quote as settled fact in a meeting.
Why the workload makes the search worse

Searching is not the worst harm. The bigger cost shows up in patient care. A 2002 JAMA study covered 10,184 staff nurses and 232,342 surgical patients in 168 Pennsylvania hospitals. Each extra patient per nurse carried higher odds of 30-day mortality (1.07). It also carried higher odds of burnout (1.23) and job dissatisfaction (1.15).

The study shows association, not cause. It is old, but it is still widely cited. Its message for you is simple. When staffing is thin, every minute of hunting is a minute you do not have at the bedside.

Turnover adds to the load. A secondary summary of the 2026 NSI report puts RN turnover at 17.6% for calendar 2025, and a cost of $60,090 for each bedside RN lost. The original PDF could not be read, so confirm those figures with NSI before you quote them. Every new hire needs time to learn where things live.
A worked example: finding one medication policy

Here is a search you might run mid-shift. A patient is on an IV pump, and the alarm is one you do not recognize. You need the policy for that alarm, and you need it now. Follow these steps in Chrome on your Mac.

items: Press ⌘L to jump to the address bar, or click your policy library bookmark if you saved one.
Type one short phrase from the policy title, such as IV pump alarm. Skip full sentences.
Scan the results for the newest approved version. Ignore drafts and anything marked superseded.
Open the policy, press ⌘F, and type alarm to jump to the section you need.
Read the revision date and the effective date before you act on it.
Press ⌘D to bookmark the page if it is the one your unit uses.

blocks.text: Notice what the steps leave out. You did not browse the home page or open five folders. The short phrase did the work. If the first search returns nothing, change one word, not the whole phrase. Try IV pump instead of IV pump alarm, then check the results again.

The edge case is the date. Policy libraries often hold old and new versions side by side. A saved PDF from last year can look official and still be wrong. When you find two versions, use the one with the newest approved date. If the dates conflict, ask your charge nurse before you act.
Search habits that work on most intranets

items: Search the policy number first. If you know it, it is usually the most exact match.
Use the title words from the policy, since the library is most likely to match its own vocabulary.
Keep the phrase short. A few key words beat a full question.
Try the word your hospital uses for the same thing, such as medication for drug or med.
Check the filter or category options on the library page before you give up.

blocks.text: Use Spotlight for policy files you already saved

Spotlight searches files and apps on your Mac. It does not search your hospital intranet. Use it once a policy is saved to your Downloads or Documents folder. Press ⌘Space to open Spotlight, then start typing. Press ⌘2 to limit results to files.

A few more Spotlight tricks help. Type kind:pdfs to show only PDFs. Press Space on a result to preview it with Quick Look. Hold ⌘ while you select a result to show it in Finder. That last step helps when you need the folder, not the file.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. It lives in the notch. Hold ⌥⌘, which is Option and Command together, and ask about anything on screen. Lazur looks at the screen while you hold the shortcut, points at things, and answers out loud.

Ask where something is and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. That helps when the search box is hard to spot on a busy intranet page. Ask how to do something and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click. You stay in control of every click.

Lazur does not click buttons, edit files, or operate other apps for you. It is not a plugin or add-in for any app, so it does not connect to your hospital's policy system. Research runs in Lazur's own Chrome tabs. Do not treat it as a search of your intranet.
Mistakes that waste the most time

items: Searching from the home page first. The library link is usually one click further.
Typing full questions into search. Many search boxes match words, not whole questions.
Trusting a saved copy without checking its date.
Asking a colleague before checking the policy. Colleagues remember old rules too.
Pasting policy text into a personal chat or email. Check your employer's rules first.

blocks.title: Patient data and your employer's rules
blocks.text: Policies rarely contain patient data, but the screens around them can. Before you hold ⌥⌘ over a screen with a patient name or record number, check your employer's rules on AI tools. Follow those rules first, every time.
Privacy and what Lazur sends

Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Your audio and the screenshot are sent to AI providers to answer you. They are not stored there. Content is never used to train AI models. Those facts help, but they do not replace your employer's policy on data.
What to do next

Start small. Today, find the policy library, bookmark it, and note its link in a Word index. Tomorrow, practice a short-phrase search on a policy you already know. Keep the habit for a week, and the next search will feel shorter. If you want help while you work, try the free trial on your own Mac, [download Lazur](/download).

Ask your unit educator which policies come up most, then build your index around those. For the index itself, see [Word for nurses on Mac](/for/nurses/word). For policy update emails, see [Outlook for nurses on Mac](/for/nurses/outlook).

faq.question: Where do hospital policies usually live?
faq.answer: Most hospitals keep policies in a document library on the intranet. It may be called a policy manual or a knowledge base. Ask your unit educator or charge nurse for the exact link. Bookmark it once in Chrome, so you never have to search for the search page again.

faq.question: Can Spotlight search my hospital intranet?
faq.answer: No. Spotlight searches files and apps on your Mac. Use it for policy PDFs you have already downloaded. Press ⌘Space, press ⌘2 to limit results to files, or type kind:pdfs to show only PDFs.

faq.question: What if two versions of the same policy show up?
faq.answer: Check the revision date, the effective date, and any status line such as draft or superseded. Use the newest approved version. If the dates conflict or the status is unclear, ask your charge nurse or unit educator before you act.

faq.question: Can Lazur find the policy on my intranet for me?
faq.answer: Lazur can point at the search box and draw a circle around it on your screen. It can guide you one click at a time. It does not click for you, and it is not a plugin for your intranet. Research runs in Lazur's own Chrome tabs.

faq.question: Is it safe to hold Option and Command over a policy page?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you, and they are not stored there. Your employer decides whether that is allowed. Do not hold the shortcut when patient details are on screen unless your employer permits it.

faq.question: Does Lazur work on Windows?
faq.answer: Not yet. Lazur runs on the Mac, on Apple silicon and Intel models. Windows is planned, but it is not available. You can check the [pricing page](/pricing) and the [download page](/download) for current details.

faq.question: Does Chrome Find work on PDFs?
faq.answer: Chrome Find works on most web pages and on PDFs open in Chrome. Press ⌘F, type the word you need, and use the arrows to step through matches. If a PDF does not respond, open it in Preview and use the search field there.

costs.title: Time lost in the middle of a task
costs.text: A policy search rarely happens at a calm moment. You are usually in the middle of a med pass, a handoff, or a charting task. When you leave that task to search, you also lose your place in it. Getting back to the same spot can cost as much time as the search itself.

costs.title: Interruptions for your colleagues
costs.text: When the search fails, you ask someone. In the single-hospital survey, nurses relied mainly on colleagues, supervisors and doctors for health information. Your question then lands on a charge nurse who is also busy. Ask only after a fast search has failed.

costs.title: Acting on an outdated version
costs.text: The worst cost is a wrong answer. A saved PDF from an earlier year can look official, with a familiar title and header. If it has been replaced, following it can mean a care step that no longer matches current practice. Check the date and the approval status every time, especially for medications and alarms.

costs.title: Frustration that adds up
costs.text: In the same survey, 43% of nurses were dissatisfied with the information they received. A small daily annoyance adds up across a year. It can make a unit feel harder to work on than it needs to be. Better personal habits will not fix the system, but they lower the daily load.

causes.title: One policy, several homes
causes.text: The same policy can sit in a shared drive, a unit folder, an email attachment, and the intranet library. Each copy may carry a different title. Search finds some of them and misses others. You are not bad at searching. The system has more doors than it should.

causes.title: Search matches words, not questions
causes.text: Intranet search often matches titles and exact words. A question like what do I do when the pump beeps may find nothing. A title like IV pump alarm management finds the policy at once. That gap between how you think and how the library names things is a common reason searches fail.

causes.title: Saved copies go stale
causes.text: People download policies to a desktop folder, then forget where they came from. The copy looks right for months. When the policy changes, the old file stays behind. Spotlight on your Mac then finds the old copy first, because it is the one you saved.

causes.title: No time to learn the system
causes.text: When you are too busy to search, you rarely get time to learn where the library lives. In the single-hospital survey, 42.6% of nurses said they were too busy to find time to search for information. The search system never gets learned, so each new search starts from zero.

causes.title: Colleagues become the search engine
causes.text: The same survey found that 25% of nurses said information was inaccessible to them. Nurses relied mainly on people. People are fast and kind. They are also not always current, and a colleague's memory of a rule can be a version behind.

fixes.title: Bookmark the library once
fixes.text: Find the policy library, then press ⌘D to bookmark it. In Chrome, show the bookmarks bar with View > Always Show Bookmarks Bar. The library is then one click away on every shift. Add the policies you use most to that bar too.

fixes.title: Search by policy number first
fixes.text: If the policy has a number, search for it first. Numbers match exactly, so the result list stays short. Copy the number from the policy header into a note on your Mac. Then you can paste it into the search box without retyping.

fixes.title: Search with the title's own words
fixes.text: Open one policy and copy a few words from its title. Search with those words, not with your own wording. If the results come back empty, change one word and search again. Do not rewrite the whole query.

fixes.title: Check the dates before you act
fixes.text: Look for the revision date, the effective date, and any status line such as draft, superseded, or retired. Use the newest approved version. If two versions conflict, ask your charge nurse or unit educator before you act, and note who confirmed it.

fixes.title: Use Chrome Find for long policies
fixes.text: Long policies are hard to scan. Press ⌘F in Chrome, type the word you need, and use the arrows to step through the matches. This works on policy web pages and on PDFs open in Chrome. It saves you from scrolling past the section you need.

fixes.title: Keep a one-page index in Word
fixes.text: Make a Word document called Policy index. List each policy with its library link and its number, one line per policy. Save it in a folder you open every shift. The index is yours, so it can use your unit's shorthand.

fixes.title: Use Spotlight for files you saved
fixes.text: For policy files already on your Mac, press ⌘Space and type a few words. Press ⌘2 to limit results to files, or type kind:pdfs. Press Space on a result to preview it with Quick Look. Spotlight searches your Mac, not the intranet, so use it for copies you already have.

fixes.title: Ask for a short index from your educator
fixes.text: Your unit educator or charge nurse often knows which policies come up most. Ask for a short list with links. Then add it to your bookmarks and your Word index. One conversation can save many searches later.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Find and bookmark the library
plan.text: Open the intranet in Chrome and find the policy library link. Press ⌘D to bookmark it. Turn on the bookmarks bar from View > Always Show Bookmarks Bar. Ask your unit educator which policies come up most.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Start a one-page index
plan.text: Open Word and create a document called Policy index. Add one line for each policy you use, with its title, library link and policy number. Keep the file in a folder you open every shift.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Practice short searches
plan.text: Pick one policy you already know. Search for it with its policy number, then with two or three words from its title. Compare the results and notice which search shows the newest version first.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Check dates and versions
plan.text: Open one policy you use often. Read the revision date, the effective date, and the status line. Write the date next to its entry in your Word index. If something does not match what your unit does, ask the charge nurse.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Clear out stale copies
plan.text: Look in Downloads, Desktop and your unit folder for old policy PDFs. Move them into a folder named Old. Do not delete anything until someone has checked it. Use Spotlight with ⌘2 and kind:pdfs to find them quickly.
